hints: Expand $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ by counting all carbon and hydrogen atoms, remembering each $\text{CH}_{2}$ contributes one carbon and two hydrogens.
walkthrough:
Expand the condensed formula**
Think of $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ as a short chain written in shorthand. You have a $\text{CH}_{3}$ at each end and two $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups in the middle. Adding carbons gives $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$ carbons in total.

hints: First work out the full molecular formula of H from $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$, then check if the C to H ratio can be simplified to its lowest whole numbers.
walkthrough:
Find the molecular formula first**
Count carefully from $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$. The $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}$ part is $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}$, plus $\text{CH}_{2}$, plus $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$ which is $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{7}$. Adding gives $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$ in total, which is 2,2,4-trimethylpentane.

Simplify to the empirical formula**
Empirical means the simplest whole number ratio. Both 8 and 18 divide by 2, so $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$ simplifies to $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}$. This is one of the few alkanes where molecular and empirical formulas are different, so do not just copy the molecular formula.

hints: Identify the longest carbon chain in J and note where the OH group sits, then recall that in skeletal formulas each bend is a carbon and hydrogens on carbon are hidden but OH is shown.
walkthrough:
Read the displayed structure as a chain**
The structure shown is $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH(OH)CH}_{3}$, which is 3-methylbutan-2-ol. The longest chain has 4 carbons, with an OH on the second carbon and an extra methyl branch on the third carbon.

Convert to skeletal shorthand**
Draw a zigzag of 4 lines for the butane backbone. At the second vertex from one end add an OH group, and at the next vertex add a short line for the methyl branch. Remember to show the O and H of the OH group explicitly, but hide all C-H hydrogens.
Final answer: Skeletal formula of $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH(OH)CH}_{3}$, 3-methylbutan-2-ol: a four carbon zigzag chain with a methyl branch on carbon 3 and an OH group on carbon 2.

hints: Use the molecular formula $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$ for H and recall complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives only $\text{CO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, then balance C, then H, then O last.
walkthrough:
Set up the products and balance C and H**
Complete combustion means plenty of oxygen, so $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$ gives $\text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ only. Balance carbon first: 8 carbons need $8\text{CO}_{2}$. Balance hydrogen next: 18 hydrogens need $9\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

Balance oxygen**
Now count oxygens on the right: $(8 \times 2) + (9 \times 1) = 25$ oxygen atoms, so you need $25/2$ or $12\frac{1}{2}$ $\text{O}_{2}$ on the left. This gives $$\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18} + 12\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 8\text{CO}_{2} + 9\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Think about what happens to elemental sulfur or sulfur compounds when a fossil fuel is burned in excess oxygen.
Link the gaseous combustion product of sulfur to its well known environmental effect when it dissolves in rainwater.
walkthrough:
Follow the sulfur on burning**
Sulfur impurities burn just like carbon does. Sulfur plus oxygen forms sulfur dioxide gas: $$\text{S} + \text{O}_{2} \rightarrow \text{SO}_{2}$$ This gas escapes into the atmosphere with the other flue gases.

Connect sulfur dioxide to acid rain**
In the air $\text{SO}_{2}$ dissolves in water droplets and is further oxidised to form sulfurous acid and sulfuric acid. This acid rain lowers the pH of lakes, leaches nutrients from soil, corrodes limestone buildings and harms living things.

Final answer: Sulfur burns to form sulfur dioxide, $\text{SO}_{2}$.
Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which damages buildings, kills aquatic life and harms trees.

hints: Sort G, H and J by type: G and H are both alkanes while J is an alcohol, so decide which comparison is alkane to alkane and which involves a different functional group.
For G ($\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}$) versus H ($\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$), compare the number of electrons and the type of intermolecular force they both rely on.
For J, look for the O-H group and recall the strongest type of intermolecular force that this group allows between molecules.
Link stronger intermolecular forces to the amount of thermal energy needed to separate molecules when boiling.
walkthrough:
Separate the two effects**
You have two alkanes, G and H, and one alcohol, J. So compare G with H first using the same type of force, then explain why J is highest using a different, stronger force. Boiling never breaks covalent bonds, it only overcomes forces between molecules.

Explain H higher than G**
Both G and H are non-polar alkanes, so the only forces between their molecules are London dispersion forces. H is $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$ while G is $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}$, so an H molecule has many more electrons. The larger electron cloud is more easily polarised to form temporary dipoles, giving stronger London forces in H. Hence H boils at $99^{\circ}\text{C}$ compared to $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ for G.

Explain J highest of all**
J is $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ with an O-H group. Between J molecules there is hydrogen bonding in addition to London forces. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than London forces, so J needs the most energy to separate its molecules, giving the highest boiling point of $112^{\circ}\text{C}$ even though J is smaller than H.

Tie energy to boiling point**
Boiling happens when molecules have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractions holding them in the liquid. Stronger attractions need more heat input, so the order of force strength, G weakest then H then J strongest, directly matches the order of boiling points.

Final answer: H has stronger London dispersion (van der Waals) forces than G because H ($\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{18}$) has more electrons than G ($\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}$).
J has hydrogen bonding between molecules, which is stronger than London dispersion forces.
Stronger intermolecular forces require more thermal energy to overcome, so boiling points increase G < H < J.

hints: Recognise the change from C-Cl in 2-chloro-3-methylbutane to C-OH in J as substitution of Cl by OH, and recall which aqueous reagent supplies $\text{OH}^{-}$ for this hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Spot the substitution**
You are going from $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{11}\text{Cl}$ to an alcohol, so $\text{Cl}$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$. This is hydrolysis by nucleophilic substitution. The standard reagent is aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, with heating, where water as solvent favours substitution to the alcohol rather than elimination.
